title: Russia’s Security State Will Not Abandon Dark Arts
content:
There is much talk about peace in Ukraine as US-brokered talks continue, and much skepticism. But if Vladimir Putin does sign a deal, there is one rarely voiced but critical question worth asking: how will Russian intelligence agencies respond?  

The answer? It would taste like poison to the Russian security state. At the very least, it would refuse to stop increasingly aggressive shadow war operations abroad. A pause is possible, but renunciation of the sabotage, political assassination, and other dark arts is unimaginable. 

How do we know? Look at recent history. 

When the KGB-orchestrated coup d’état failed in Moscow in August 1991, leading to the swift collapse of the Soviet Union, Russian President Boris Yeltsin appeared fully committed to reforming the KGB. He went as far as splitting a monstrous, all-encompassing organization into several agencies.  

But the division responsible for its offensive capabilities proved the most resistant to change, and the most resourceful.

title: NATO: The Shift from Budgets to Battlefields
content:
The alliance’s next test will not be measured in percentages of GDP; it will be judged on its ability to defend its territory, defeat aggression, and sustain military operations against a capable adversary. 

For too long, discussions about NATO’s effectiveness have been dominated by spending. The argument has been politically useful, particularly in persuading European capitals to invest more, but it has obscured a more important question: what can NATO’s forces actually accomplish? 

It’s an important distinction. Spending is an input. Military capability is an output. Operational readiness determines whether it can be employed when needed. 

At the 2025 Hague Summit, NATO allies committed to investing 5% of GDP into defense and security by 2035. The commitment marked a substantial advance from the previous 2% benchmark, and by the July 2026 Ankara Summit, European members and Canada had increased defense investment by more than $139bn. 

Europe has underinvested in its defense for decades, so the commitments in the face of a deteriorating security environment matter, but NATO cannot afford to confuse financial progress with military effectiveness.

title: Blood in the Black Sea: What Can Turkey Do?
content:
The Black Sea is now the world’s most dangerous body of water. Hundreds of attacks on merchant vessels have left littoral neighbors wondering how to respond to an issue fraught with risk. Turkish, Bulgarian, and Romanian defense ministers met in Sofia on October 28 to discuss possible approaches.

From January to September, more than 570 ships were attacked in the Black Sea, with at least 40 sailors killed, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The campaign has made the Black Sea the world’s most dangerous commercial shipping route, ahead of the Strait of Hormuz, where there have been 24 deaths since the start of the year.

The upsurge in violence has disrupted trade operations and increased security concerns, particularly for Turkey, which has critical energy assets in the basin and controls access to the sea under the Montreux Convention.

title: Nordics Show the Way on Arctic Defense
content:
Since Finland and Sweden joined NATO in the wake of Russia’s all-out attack on Ukraine, the region’s defenses have been enormously strengthened on the alliance’s northern flank, not least because their accession unlocked new levels of regional cooperation.  

Until Helsinki and Stockholm took the plunge, the original Nordic NATO members of Denmark, Iceland and Norway, had been wary of creating duplicate structures through separate Nordic cooperation.  

But Finland and Sweden hit the ground running when they joined the alliance and are already hosting new NATO arrangements such as the Multi Corps Land Component Command in Eastern Finland, the Forward Land Force (FLF) in Northern Finland, and logistics headquarters in Sweden.  

Building on longstanding bilateral defense cooperation between Finland and Sweden, FLF Finland is led by Sweden, with contributions from the other three Nordic countries and the European nuclear weapons powers, France and the UK. Italy and potentially Spain may also join.

title: Going Underground: Ukraine’s Kids Study Without Sunlight
content:
When Olena Kozachenko chose a school for her son in Kyiv, she had two requirements: it had to be close to home, and it had to have a good bomb shelter. Not academic rankings or extracurricular activities. A bomb shelter.

Yaromyr, eight, has only ever attended school during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. His Kyiv school was the one his mother and grandmother had attended. Some teachers still recognized Olena. Yet his school days would look nothing like his mother’s during the years of peace. Even his first teacher had been displaced by war, leaving Kostiantynivka in the Donetsk region to teach in the capital city.

For two years, Olena says, things were relatively manageable. Power cuts disrupted routines, but generators arrived, and school meals resumed. Then, in September, constant air raid alerts made moving children repeatedly between classrooms and shelter impractical. The youngest pupils began spending entire school days underground.

“There were about 70 children in one space,” Olena recalls. “It was incredibly noisy. They didn’t go outside. They didn’t see the sun. They were in the shelter constantly.” They learned, drew, and ate at the same desks.

title: Russia: The Primary Threat in the Arctic
content:
As the ice recedes in the Arctic, a new and contested area is fast emerging: the circumpolar region is now becoming key in the modern geopolitical contest. The September agreement between the US, Denmark, and Greenland is an important first step in shaping a new Arctic military architecture.  

The Arctic is present too in the shadows cast by the Iran war on the Strait of Hormuz and other critical trade chokepoints, amid proposed alternative maritime shipping routes through the region. It is also at the forefront of climate insecurity, with permafrost thawing and waterways opening.   

The Trump administration is correct in assessing that Russian ships are present “all over” the Arctic. Yet if Russian surface deployments are not apparent close to Greenland, they are indeed noticeable from the Barents Sea to the Pacific Arctic. In fact, Russia remains the primary security threat to US and NATO interests in the region, and everyone would do well to remember it. 

A CEPA report, Frontline Arctic: The Evolution of Russia’s Military Posture in a Changing Arctic, examines the threat that Russia’s military posture and activities continue to pose to the United States, NATO, and their regional allies.

title: Russia’s Leaders: Children of a Dead Age
content:
Russia is led by Vladimir Putin, Sergei Lavrov, and Valery Gerasimov, who are 74, 76, and 71 years old. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, heralding the end of the Soviet empire, they were already adults of 37, 39, and 34.

Their worldviews were formed in the USSR, and they still long for the days when their country oppressed Central and Eastern Europe, had influence across the globe, and was one of the world’s two superpowers.

Ukraine, in contrast, is led by much younger leaders. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is 48; Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43; and Olha Stefanishyna, the former ambassador to the US, 41. Presidential aide Kyrylo Budanov is 40, while former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov is only 35.

When the Wall came, Zelenskyy was 11, Drapatyi six, Stefanishyna four, and Budanov three. Fedorov had not yet been born. Their worldviews were developed in a free and independent Ukraine. They do not long for a return to the Soviet Union.

This age difference also explains why both sides are so adamant about winning.

title: Poland’s Endless Battle for Justice
content:
More than a decade of conflict has deprived Poland of an accepted constitutional arbiter. Victory in the latest confrontation, whoever wins it, will not restore one. 

On October 30, Poland’s president aborted a flight to Senegal mid-route as police blockaded the Constitutional Tribunal and rival judges fought for control. By November 4, the standoff had unraveled into competing criminal allegations. Beneath the spectacle lies a fundamental crisis of authority: state institutions no longer agree on whose decisions constitute law. 

The tribunal decides whether legislation contravenes the constitution and settles disputes over constitutional powers. Its 15 judges serve non-renewable nine-year terms. Parliament’s lower house, the Sejm, elects them. The president administers their statutory oaths. That distinction matters: the constitution gives him no power to block parliament’s choice.

title: Managing Russia’s Military-Industrial Degradation: Navigating Wartime Industrial Constraints, Stockpile Exhaustion, and Hardware Attrition
content:
• This paper assesses Russia’s near-term domestic defense-industrial capacity and the ability of the military-industrial complex (OPK) to meet the increasing demands of the war against Ukraine.
  • Four years into the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has not solved the problem of sustaining wartime production. Instead, the Kremlin has only postponed addressing the OPK’s many problems.
  • Output constraints are increasingly defining the OPK’s future: exhaustion (specifically, the depletion of existing stockpiles and the constant need to repair damaged equipment and refurbish Soviet-legacy hardware taken out of storage) and attrition (the limited ability to produce new military hardware domestically faster than it is consumed).
  • Finding a balance between the two constraints has allowed the armed forces to continue fielding equipment, but it has also accelerated the depletion of Soviet-era reserves. However, the constant trade-off has become a systemic condition that defines the current and future trajectory of the military industry. The OPK cannot indefinitely compensate for battlefield losses through repair and refurbishment alone.
snippet: This paper assesses Russia’s near-term domestic defense-industrial capacity and the ability of the military-industrial complex (OPK) to meet the increasing demands of the war against Ukraine.

title: Data Center Attacks Matter But Not in the Way We Thought
content:
Within hours of the attacks, it was claimed the strikes had done something years of counter-disinformation efforts had struggled to achieve by taking Russian propaganda bots offline. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said social media had become easier to navigate, with fewer bots, less division, and fewer provocations. 

Officials pointed to apparent interruptions in Russian automated information networks, while commentators began asking if Ukraine had found a way to physically disrupt the infrastructure underpinning Russia’s information war. 

However, while researchers have found evidence of temporary disruption to some automated Russian networks, there is little evidence that the strikes degraded its broader influence operations.  

Moscow’s information operations include a wide range of tools, including various servers, cloud platforms, and residential internet connections. Moreover, the affected data centers supported a wide range of digital services. The disruptions observed in automated systems cannot be equated with a weakening of the Kremlin’s entire propaganda apparatus.

title: Hybrid War Makes High North a Contest for NATO
content:
This article forms part of a CEPA series on the new strategic landscape in the Arctic.

“High North, low tension” is becoming a comforting slogan rather than a credible strategy. Russia’s war on Ukraine, NATO’s northern enlargement, and growing Russia-China cooperation have eroded Arctic exceptionalism.

A conventional Russia-NATO war is not inevitable, but Moscow is likely to continue using sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference, and provocations to challenge sovereignty and test allied resolve. The alliance’s challenge is to defend the High North against aggression deliberately kept below the threshold of war.

Moscow’s Arctic strategy centers on protecting its nuclear deterrent, controlling the Northern Sea Route, and restricting NATO’s access to sensitive Russian territory. The Kola Peninsula, which abuts Norway and Finland and is home to key Northern Fleet and sea-based nuclear assets, is central to these objectives.

The war in Ukraine has weakened some of Russia’s conventional capabilities, while Finland and Sweden’s NATO accession has heightened Moscow’s sense of exposure, a combination that may encourage greater reliance on asymmetric operations.

creator: Sara George

title: Midterm Fallout: AI and Data Centers Take Center Stage
content:
An unpopular war in Iran. Rising prices for gas and groceries. Anger over data centers. These three issues combined to propel the Democrats to a historic midterm victory, raising the prospect that the new Congress will pursue data center moratoriums and AI safety regulation. 

Public pressure for action is mounting. According to exit polling, 56% of voters stated that AI and data centers represented a “crucial or major factor” in their ballot decision. Data centers are blamed for rising electricity bills. Democrats weaponized the issue, spending more than $100 million on ads framing Republicans as friends of data centers. They even sent personalized leaflets to Texas voters near a proposed data center site, warning that Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton would give the project a green light. Paxton lost.

title: How Europe Should Read the US Midterms
content:
The US midterm elections delivered a striking rebuke to President Trump. But Europeans, including Ukrainians, should be cautious not to over-interpret the implications for his foreign policy.

This election was not about Europe, nor Ukraine, nor foreign policy in general, other than as a metaphor for leadership. It was about prices, the economy, the self-inflicted war against Iran, and the general sense that Trump has lost the thread.

True, most Americans disagree with President Trump’s approach to Russia, Ukraine, NATO, tariffs, and more. And Democrats will have significant majorities in both the House and the Senate, beginning in January. But Trump remains President and therefore has significant leeway in foreign policy, as well as a veto over legislation passed by Congress. And there is no indication that the President will suddenly change his views.
